architecture.mechanism: Geothermal energy-based drying — the abstract identifies geothermal heat as a renewable energy source for drying/evaporation processes, and reports that such renewable and hybrid drying systems lower energy demand relative to conventional methods.
architecture.intervention: Fit the existing wellhead cyclone separators and flash-vessel internals with a bolt-in, non-welded (clamp/blanket) geothermal drying assembly: during the 4-day annual outage, divert a side-stream of the field's own brine/steam — kept below 180 °C — through removable heating panels to thermally dry the wet calcite and silica-gel deposits on the internals; drying-induced shrinkage plus differential thermal expansion cracks and de-bonds the scale from the vessel walls so it can be scraped/spalled out with on-site equipment. No pressure-boundary welding, geometry unchanged, brine chemistry (Ca up to 900 mg/L) unaffected since it is a removal route rather than a chemistry change.
architecture.expected_effect: Restores separator internal flow area and cyclone performance, cutting the 6–11% quarterly thermal-output loss; reduces fouling-driven pressure drop between wellhead and downstream silica zone; the procedure is contained within the 4-day outage using on-site tooling.
architecture.falsification_test: On a full-scale mock cyclone section, grow representative calcite + silica deposits from field brine at 900 mg/L Ca, then run the clamp-on geothermal drying cycle with brine-side temperature held below 180 °C; measure (a) scale adhesion strength before/after drying, (b) mass of scale removable by standardized mechanical scraping versus a wet (undried) control, (c) restoration of original flow area per unit labor-hour. Falsified if dried-section removal is not at least 2x the wet control, if any panel exceeds 180 °C, or if the cycle cannot be completed inside the 4-day outage.
